zocalo.today: Stand by the flagpole and scan the plaza: the cathedral on one side, Palacio Nacional on another. It’s hard to imagine the star of this story is something you cannot see. Look for a monument to Independence. Where is it? That’s where the story begins.
zocalo.history: In 1843, Santa Anna backed a monument to Independence. It was meant to have a column and a statue; only the base, the zócalo, remained. The project stalled, but its nickname stuck. The city ended up naming the entire plaza after an unfinished job.
zocalo.twist: In 2017, INAH archaeologists found part of the platform: just eight meters across and 28 centimeters high. A tiny base for such an enormous plaza. You cannot see it today: after documenting it, the team protected the remains beneath the paving.

ehecatl.today: You’re thinking about Line 1 or Line 2 when there it is: a small round shrine. Stairs, corridors, people coming and going. The scene asks you to slow down. At Pino Suárez, changing trains can also mean changing centuries.
ehecatl.history: The National Museum of Anthropology places the discovery during Metro excavations in 1969. The round temple, on a rectangular platform, is associated with Ehécatl-Quetzalcóatl. Its form may evoke whirlwinds—a possibility the museum discusses, not a certainty.
ehecatl.twist: The shrine preserves earlier structures inside it. When renewing a temple, the Mexica could build over its predecessor. What looks like a small ruin is stacked history: the Metro above, a temple in view, and other eras within.

revolucion.today: From Plaza de la República, look at the four arches and the dome. Now imagine a building around them. A much bigger building. What dominates Tabacalera today was meant to be just one part of an ambitious Legislative Palace.
revolucion.history: The Revolution interrupted the Porfirian project. Its steel structure stood abandoned for years. As demolition began, Carlos Obregón Santacilia proposed saving the dome of the Hall of Lost Steps and giving it a new purpose. The transformation took place between 1933 and 1938.
revolucion.twist: The building intended to house political power ended up remembering the revolution that disrupted the project. It also became a mausoleum: Venustiano Carranza arrived in 1942. Look at the dome again. It is more than an unfinished piece; it is a second life.

chapultepec.today: Among the trees and paths, a stone reservoir bears an irresistible name: the Baths of Moctezuma. It is easy to picture the ruler’s private pool. Before accepting the legend, look at how it was built. The water has another story.
chapultepec.history: INAH distinguishes the pre-Hispanic reservoir from public baths built opposite it in 1870. The reservoir supplied water; it was not Moctezuma’s private pool. The Casa Baños de Chapultepec, meanwhile, became known for waters believed to be curative.
chapultepec.twist: The nineteenth-century baths disappeared, and the royal name attached itself to the surviving reservoir. In 2018, archaeologists found remains of three pools from the bathing establishment. Two places, two eras, and one nickname that tangled them together.
